summary: Defines Opaque LSAs for OSPF, a generalized way to carry application-specific information using standard flooding, so OSPF can be extended later. It adds a mechanism for validating AS-scope Opaque LSAs originated outside a router's area. It replaces RFC 2370. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: OSPF routers share maps. An opaque LSA is a sealed note that routers pass along that other programs can use later.

questions: what is an ospf opaque lsa
what are type 9 10 and 11 lsas in ospf
how does ospf flood opaque lsas
subtitle: A generic container for OSPF to flood extra, application-specific data with the normal link-state machinery.

tldr.problem: OSPF needed a general way to carry new kinds of information to other routers without defining a new LSA type each time.
tldr.mechanism: Opaque LSAs (types 9, 10 and 11) hold a standard LSA header plus application-specific data, and the type sets the flooding scope: link-local, area-local or the whole AS.
tldr.outcome: This RFC obsoletes RFC 2370 and adds a way to check that the originator of an AS-scope Opaque LSA is still reachable, which avoids using stale data.

today: RFC 5250 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2370, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
OSPF has been widely deployed and extended with many options. RFC 5250 defines Opaque LSAs, a new class of link state advertisements meant to make OSPF extensible in the future. The information they carry may be used directly by OSPF or by another application that wants to distribute data through the OSPF domain. Exactly how they are used is out of scope.

An Opaque LSA is a standard LSA header followed by a 32-bit aligned, application-specific information field. It is distributed with the normal link-state database flooding mechanism. The RFC envisions an implementation offering an application interface to encapsulate and send or receive application data, and to tell the application when previously received information changes validity after a topology change.
sections.eli5: It adds a general-purpose envelope to OSPF, so new kinds of messages can ride the same delivery system.

sections.title: Types and Flooding Scope
sections.content:
Opaque LSAs are link-state types 9, 10 and 11, and the type identifies the flooding scope, the range of topological distribution.

  • Type 9 is link-local. It is not flooded beyond the local (sub)network.
  • Type 10 is area-local. It is not flooded beyond the borders of its area.
  • Type 11 is flooded throughout the Autonomous System, like AS-External (type 5) LSAs. It is flooded through transit areas, not flooded into stub areas or NSSAs, and not originated by routers into their connected stub areas or NSSAs.

The link-state ID splits into an Opaque type (the first 8 bits) and a type-specific ID (the remaining 24 bits). Both sender and receiver are responsible for scope. A receiver must not accept an Opaque LSA that violates the scope, for example a type 11 LSA in a stub area or NSSA.
sections.eli5: The type number says how far the envelope may travel: just the next door, just your neighborhood, or the whole city.

sections.title: Flooding Rules and Capability
sections.content:
Normal OSPF flooding from RFC 2328 applies except where this RFC changes it. A type 9 LSA received on an interface other than the target interface MUST be discarded and not acknowledged. A type 10 LSA whose area differs from the target interface's area MUST be discarded and not acknowledged. A type 11 LSA MUST NOT be flooded out an interface in a stub area or NSSA, and one received there MUST be discarded and not acknowledged.

Opaque LSAs only go to routers that understand them. A neighbor is opaque-capable if and only if it sets the O-bit in the Options field of its Database Description packets, which a router learns during the Database Exchange process. Opaque LSAs MUST be placed on the retransmission lists of opaque-capable neighbors and MUST NOT be placed on those of other neighbors. If a non-capable router gets one by multicast, it simply discards it.

Information from received Opaque LSAs SHOULD only be used when the originating router is reachable.
sections.eli5: Routers announce whether they can read these envelopes. Envelopes are only handed to routers that said yes, and each one must stay inside its allowed zone.

sections.title: Neighbor State Machine Change
sections.content:
The neighbor state machine of RFC 2328 stays the same except for one action: state ExStart, event NegotiationDone, where the Database summary list is built. The router MUST list the contents of its entire area link-state database, which now includes type 9 and type 10 Opaque LSAs in the area structure, and type 11 Opaque LSAs alongside AS External LSAs in the global structure.

Some entries MUST be left out: AS External and type 11 LSAs for a virtual neighbor or a stub area or NSSA, type 9 LSAs whose interface is not the neighbor's interface, and any LSA at MaxAge, which goes onto the retransmission list instead. The RFC also adds an opaque capability item to the global data structures and a neighbor option recording the neighbor's opaque capability.
sections.eli5: When two routers first compare their notebooks, they now skip any envelope that does not belong in that conversation.

sections.title: Inter-Area Validation of AS-Scope LSAs
sections.content:
A type 11 LSA has a problem: if its originator goes out of service, routers in other areas cannot see this and may use stale information for up to 60 minutes. Types 9 and 10 do not have this problem, because reachability can be checked within their scope.

The fix reuses what OSPF already does for type 5 LSAs: AS border information in ASBR Summary (type 4) LSAs. An originator of AS-scope Opaque LSAs advertises itself as an ASBR and MUST follow the Options field E-bit rules of RFC 2328. A receiver of a type 11 LSA MUST look up routing table entries for the originating ASBR, MUST do nothing with the LSA if the ASBR is unreachable, and MUST stop using all Opaque LSAs from that originator once it is found unreachable. This does not apply to stub areas or NSSAs.
sections.eli5: If the person who sent a note leaves town, far-away routers could keep trusting the note. Now they check the sender is still around.

sections.title: The Opaque LSA Format and Options Field
sections.content:
The Opaque LSA header holds LS age, Options, the type (9, 10 or 11), an 8-bit Opaque Type, a 24-bit Opaque ID, Advertising Router, LS Sequence Number, LS checksum and Length, followed by the Opaque Information padded to 32-bit alignment.

The OSPF Options field has all 8 bits assigned: DN, O, DC, EA, N/P, MC, E and MT. This document fully describes only the O-bit, the router's willingness to receive and forward Opaque LSAs. Routers SHOULD clear unrecognized option bits when sending and SHOULD ignore unrecognized bits when receiving. The O-bit SHOULD NOT be set, and MUST be ignored, in packets other than Database Description packets.
sections.eli5: Each envelope has a label with its age, its kind, who sent it and a check number. A row of switches says which special features a router supports.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC names two concerns: authentication of routing information, and denial of service from repeated origination or from database overflow. Both exist with or without Opaque LSA support. OSPF packets are authenticated, and the Cryptographic option, where MD5 is the only digest algorithm specified, offers significant protection against active attacks but no confidentiality. Repeated origination is limited by MinLSInterval (5 seconds) and MinLSArrival (1). Type 11 tracking reuses the type 5 ASBR mechanism, so it adds no new threats.

On compatibility, the option introduces no interoperability issues because non-capable routers discard the LSAs. However, routers implementing RFC 2370 keep using stale type 11 LSAs even when the originator uses the new inter-area procedures.
sections.eli5: Routers already check who is talking and limit how fast notes may be sent. Old routers just ignore envelopes they do not understand.
